author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 281 (right col.): expedition of 'Ubayda b. al-Harith b. al-Muttalib (first flag in Islam)
arabic: وهي أوَّل راية عقدها عليه الصلاة والسلام
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). Printed page not determined; no Wustenfeld pagination available Heading only (djvu line ~25387). Rabigh is NOT named in this passage (Thaniyyat al-Murra is).
english: During that stay in Medina the apostle sent 'Ubayda b. al-Harith b. al-Muttalib with sixty or eighty riders from the emigrants, there not being a single one of the Ansar among them. He went as far as water in the Hijaz below Thaniyyatu'l-Murra, where he encountered a large number of Quraysh. No fighting took place except that Sa'd b. Abi Waqqas shot an arrow on that day. It was the first arrow to be shot in Islam.
page: Guillaume p. 281 R; Wustenfeld 339 marked later in the same passage ('Ikrima ... (339))
what_it_says: Muhammad sent a sixty-to-eighty-man Emigrant force toward a Qurayshi group in the Hijaz; the text says no fighting took place beyond one arrow shot.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 282 (left col.): Abu Bakr's poem on 'Ubayda's raid (introduced on p. 281)
english: I swear, and I am no perjurer, / If they do not quickly repent of their error, / A valiant band will descend upon them, / Which will leave women husbandless. / It will leave dead men, with vultures wheeling round, / It will not spare the infidels as Ibn Harith did.
page: Guillaume p. 282 L; poem introduced as 'Concerning this raid Abu Bakr composed the following (340)'; W. 341 on p. 283 R
what_it_says: Abu Bakr's poem promises that a valiant band will come down on the unbelievers, leaving women husbandless and dead men for the vultures.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 282 (left col.): 'Abdullah b. al-Ziba'ra al-Sahmi's reply (Meccan poem)
english: Is a strong army which came to us / Led by 'Ubayda, called Ibn Harith in war, / That we should abandon images venerated in Mecca, / Passed on to his heirs by a noble ancestor. ... They withdrew in great fear and awe, / Pleased with the order of him who kept them back. / Had they not done so the women would have wailed,
page: Guillaume p. 282 L; no Wustenfeld marker in this stretch (lies between W. 340 and 341, inferred)
what_it_says: A Meccan poet, answering Abu Bakr, describes the Muslim force as an army that came against Mecca and made the Meccans withdraw in fear.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)

ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 283 (right col.): Hamza's expedition to the sea-shore near al-'Is
arabic: وبعث في مُقامه ذلك حَمزْةَ بن عبد المطلب بن هاشم إلى سيف البخرء من ناحية بذلك الساحل في ثلاثمئة راكب من أهل مكة. فحجز بينهم مَجْديٌ بن عَمرو الجهنيّ
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). Printed page not determined; no Wustenfeld pagination available OCR-damaged ('البخرء' for 'البحر'); the OCR line gives the 300 Meccan riders but not the thirty emigrants; check against the page image.
english: While he was staying there he sent Hamza b. 'Abdu'l-Muttalib to the sea-shore in the neighbourhood of Al-'Is (T. in the territory of Juhayna) with thirty riders from the emigrants; none of the helpers took part. He met Abu Jahl with three hundred riders from Mecca on the shore, and Majdi b. 'Amr al-Juhani intervened between them, for he was at peace with both parties. So the people separated one from another without fighting.
page: Guillaume p. 283 R; between W. 342 (p. 283 L) and W. 343 (poem after the paragraph), inferred
what_it_says: Hamza led thirty emigrants to intercept Meccans on the coast near al-'Is; a neutral ally of both sides separated them and no battle followed. The sources do not present it as a defensive posture.

ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 281 (right col.): 'the raid on Waddan' (al-Abwa'), Muhammad's first raid
arabic: غزوة ودان وهي أوّل غزواته عليه الصلاة والسلام ... ثم رجغ رسول الله ككل إلى المدينة» ولم يلق كيداًء فأقام بها بقية صفرء وصدراً من شهر ربيع الأوّل.
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). english: Then he went forth raiding in Safar at the beginning of the twelfth month from his coming to Medina (337). ... until he reached Waddan, which is the raid of al-Abwa', making for Quraysh and B. Damra b. Bakr b. 'Abd Manat b. Kinana. The B. Damra there made peace with him through their leader Makhshi b. 'Amr al-Damri. Then he returned to Medina without meeting war and remained there for the rest of Safar and the beginning of Rabi'u'l-awwal (338).
page: Guillaume p. 281 R; W. 337 marked after 'from his coming to Medina (337)'; W. 338 at the end (OCR 'CBS)')
what_it_says: Muhammad's first raid went toward Quraysh and Banu Damra; it ended in a peace with Banu Damra and no battle.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 285 (right col.): 'The raid on Buwat'
english: Then the apostle went raiding in the month of Rabi'u'l-Awwal making for Quraysh (345), until he reached Buwat in the neighbourhood of Radwa. Then he returned to Medina without fighting, and remained there for the rest of Rabi'u'l-Akhir and part of Jumada'l-Ula.
page: Guillaume p. 285 R; W. 345 marked after 'making for Quraysh (345)'
what_it_says: A second raid, in Rabi' I of 2 AH and aimed at Quraysh, reached Buwat near Radwa and returned without a battle.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 285 (right col.): 'The raid on al-'Ushayra' (treaty with Banu Mudlij)
english: Then he raided the Quraysh (346). He went by the way of B. Dinar, then by Fayfa'u-l-Khabar, and halted under a tree in the valley of Ibn Azhar called Dhatu'l-Saq. ... He made a treaty of friendship there with B. Mudlij and their allies B. Damra, and then returned to Medina without a fight.
page: Guillaume p. 285 R; W. 346 marked after 'raided the Quraysh (346)'
what_it_says: The al-'Ushayra raid is explicitly aimed at Quraysh, but it ended with a treaty of friendship with Banu Mudlij and Banu Damra and no fight.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)

ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 286 (left col.): 'The raid of Sa'd b. Abi Waqqas' to al-Kharrar
arabic: قال ابن إسحاق : وقد كان بعث رسول الله بَكةِ فيما بين ذلك من غزوة سَّعْد بن أبي وقاص في ثمانية رَمْط من المُهاجرين» فخرج حتى بلغ الخَرّار من أرض الحجازء ثم رجع ولم يلق
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). english: Meanwhile the apostle had sent Sa'd b. Abi Waqqas with eight men from the emigrants. He went as far as al-Kharrar in the Hijaz. Then he returned without fighting (347).
page: Guillaume p. 286 L; W. 347 marked after 'without fighting (347)'
what_it_says: Sa'd b. Abi Waqqas led eight emigrants to al-Kharrar and came back without a fight; Ibn Hisham notes some scholars date it after Hamza's expedition.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 286 (left col.): Kurz b. Jabir raid and 'the first raid of Badr' (Safwan)
arabic: غزوة سَفْوَان وهي غزوة بدر الأولى
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). Printed page not determined; no Wustenfeld pagination available Heading only.
english: The apostle stayed only a few nights, less than ten, in Medina when he came back from raiding Al-'Ushayra, and then Kurz b. Jabir al-Fihri raided the pasturing camels of Medina. The apostle went out in search of him (348), until he reached a valley called Safwan, in the neighbourhood of Badr. Kurz escaped him and he could not overtake him. This was the first raid of Badr.
page: Guillaume p. 286 L; W. 348 marked after 'went out in search of him (348)'
what_it_says: After Kurz b. Jabir raided Medina's pasturing camels, Muhammad pursued him to Safwan near Badr; Guillaume calls this the first raid of Badr.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 287 (right col.): the sealed letter sent with 'Abdullah b. Jahsh to Nakhla
arabic: إذا نظرت في كتابي هذا فامض حتى تنزل نَخْلة بين مكة والطائف» فترضّد بها قريشاً وتعلّم لنا من أخبارهم
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). Printed page not determined; no Wustenfeld pagination available Clean OCR; line 25945-25946 of the djvu text.
english: 'When you have read this letter of mine proceed until you reach Nakhla between Mecca and Al-Ta'if. Lie in wait there for Quraysh and find out for us what they are doing.' Having read the letter he said, 'To hear is to obey.' ... The apostle has commanded me to go to Nakhla to lie in wait there for Quraysh so as to bring him news of them.
page: Guillaume p. 287 R; no Wustenfeld marker in this stretch (W. 349 follows shortly)
what_it_says: The sealed letter ordered an eight-man party to lie in wait at Nakhla for Quraysh; the men were told not to pressure any companion to go on.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 287 (right col.): Nakhla caravan, killing of 'Amr b. al-Hadrami in the last day of Rajab
arabic: فمرّت به عيرٌ لقريش تحمل زبيباً وأدَمآ
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). Printed page not determined; no Wustenfeld pagination available Arabic covers only the caravan passing; the killing itself is not in the clean OCR.
english: A caravan of Quraysh carrying dry raisins and leather and other merchandise of Quraysh passed by them, 'Amr b. al-Hadrami (349), 'Uthman b. Abdullah b. al-Mughira and his brother Naufal the Makhzumites, and al-Hakam b. Kaysan, freedman of Hisham b. al-Mughira being among them. ... 'If you leave them alone tonight they will get into the sacred area and will be safe from you; and if you kill them, you will kill them in the sacred month,' so they were hesitant and feared to attack them. Then they encouraged each other, and decided to kill as many as they could of them and take what they had. Waqid shot 'Amr b. al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him, and 'Uthman and al-Hakam surrendered. Naufal escaped and eluded them.
page: Guillaume p. 287 R; W. 349 marked after "'Amr b. al-Hadrami (349)"
what_it_says: On the last day of Rajab, a sacred month, Muhammad's raiders attacked a Qurayshi caravan, killed 'Amr b. al-Hadrami, and took two prisoners and the goods.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 287 R (end), continuing p. 288 L: Muhammad's disavowal of the sacred-month attack
english: When they came to the apostle, he said, 'I did not order you to fight in the sacred month,' and he held the caravan and the two prisoners in suspense and refused to take anything from them. When the apostle said that, the men were in despair and thought that they were doomed.
page: Guillaume p. 287 R, bottom; no Wustenfeld marker in this stretch
what_it_says: Ibn Ishaq records Muhammad disowning the attack in the sacred month and withholding the caravan's goods, which is the source's own counter-evidence to a planned attack.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 288 (left col.): the Quraysh objection and the Jewish omen
english: ...the Quraysh said 'Muhammad and his companions have violated the sacred month, shed blood therein, taken booty, and captured men.' The Muslims in Mecca who opposed them said that they had done it in Sha'ban. The Jews turned this raid into an omen against the apostle.
page: Guillaume p. 288 L; falls between W. 349 and W. 350 (inferred)
what_it_says: The Meccan charge (breaking the sacred month) and an alternative dating claim that the raid was in Sha'ban, both recorded before the revelation response.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 288 (left col.): Guillaume's translation of Q 2:217 as the answer to the Nakhla objection
english: 'They will ask you about the sacred month, and war in it. Say, war therein is a serious matter, but keeping people from the way of God and disbelieving in Him and in the sacred mosque and driving out His people therefrom is more serious with God.' ... 'And seduction is worse than killing.' ... 'And they will not cease to fight you until they turn you back from your religion if they can.'
page: Guillaume p. 288 L; falls between W. 349 and W. 350 (inferred). Footnote reads 'Sura 2. 21?' (last digit unclear at scan resolution; the quoted text is 2:217)
what_it_says: Ibn Ishaq presents a revelation (Q 2:217) that answers the Meccan charge; the same verse also says that fighting will continue until Muslims are turned from their religion.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 289 (left col.): Abu Bakr's poem, offensive lines on Nakhla
english: Our lances drank of Ibn al-Hadrami's blood / In Nakhla when Waqid lit the flame of war, / 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah is with us, / A leather band streaming with blood restrains him.
page: Guillaume p. 289 L; W. 351 marked before the poem ('when Quraysh said ... (351)')
what_it_says: Abu Bakr's poem celebrates the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami at Nakhla and the capture of 'Uthman.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 289 (left col.): Abu Bakr's poem, first lines (Muslim grievance)
english: You count war in the holy month a grave matter, / But graver is, if one judges rightly, / Your opposition to Muhammad's teaching, and your unbelief in it, which God sees and witnesses, / Your driving God's people from His mosque / So that none can be seen worshipping Him there. / Though you defame us for killing him, / More dangerous to Islam is the sinner who envies.
page: Guillaume p. 289 L; W. 351 marked before the poem
what_it_says: The poem's grievance case: Quraysh opposed Islam and drove Muslims from the Sacred Mosque, so the sacred-month charge is hypocritical. Persecution and expulsion are the main defensive claim, presented here as a justification.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 289 R: 'The great expedition of Badr', Muhammad orders attack on Abu Sufyan's caravan
arabic: فيها أموالّهم فاخْرُجوا إليها لعل الله يُنفِلُكُموها
arabic_edition: Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Ibrahim al-Abyari, Abd al-Hafiz Shalabi (title page of scan); scan = archive.org item 04-2._20260427, file '04-2. سيرة ابن هشام_djvu.txt' (OCR). Printed page not determined; no Wustenfeld pagination available The opening words ('هذه عير قريش' before 'فيها') are OCR-damaged in the djvu text (line ~26119: 'وقال افده عدن دوسي'); the quoted tail is clean (line ~26120).
english: Then the apostle heard that Abu Sufyan b. Harb was coming from Syria with a large caravan of Quraysh, containing their money and merchandise accompanied by some thirty or forty men ... he summoned the Muslims and said, 'This is the Quraysh caravan containing their property. Go out to attack it, perhaps God will give it as a prey.' The people answered his summons, some eagerly, others reluctantly because they had not thought that the apostle would go to war.
page: Guillaume p. 289 R; W. 352 marked after the caravan's escort list ('Hisham (352)')
what_it_says: Muhammad himself orders an attack on Abu Sufyan's caravan for plunder ('perhaps God will give it as a prey'); some Muslims were reluctant because they had not expected a war.

work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq; recension of Ibn Hisham), tr. A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad (OUP, 1955)
author: Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 150/767); recension Ibn Hisham (d. 218/833)
ref: Ibn Ishaq/Guillaume p. 291 (right col.): Quraysh mobilise for Badr, comparing it to Ibn al-Hadrami's caravan
english: The men prepared quickly, saying, 'Do Muhammad and his companions think this is going to be like the caravan of Ibn al-Hadrami? By God, they will soon know that it is not so.' Every man of them either went himself or sent someone in his place.
page: Guillaume p. 291 R; no Wustenfeld marker seen in the OCR
what_it_says: The Meccans respond to the Medinan raid by mobilising for Badr and explicitly compare it to the Nakhla killing.

date: Medina, c. 2 AH (Ibn Ishaq dates it to the Nakhla aftermath)
arabic: يَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلشَّهْرِ ٱلْحَرَامِ قِتَالٍ فِيهِ ۖ قُلْ قِتَالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ ۖ وَصَدٌّ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَكُفْرٌۢ بِهِۦ وَٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ وَإِخْرَاجُ أَهْلِهِۦ مِنْهُ أَكْبَرُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ ۚ وَٱلْفِتْنَةُ أَكْبَرُ مِنَ ٱلْقَتْلِ ۗ وَلَا يَزَالُونَ يُقَـٰتِلُونَكُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَرُدُّوكُمْ عَن دِينِكُمْ إِنِ ٱسْتَطَـٰعُوا۟ ۚ وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكُمْ عَن دِينِهِۦ فَيَمُتْ وَهُوَ كَافِرٌ فَأُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ حَبِطَتْ أَعْمَـٰلُهُمْ فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ ۖ وَأُو۟لَـٰٓئِكَ أَصْحَـٰبُ ٱلنَّارِ ۖ هُمْ فِيهَا خَـٰلِدُونَ
arabic_edition: quran.com API v4, verses/by_key/2:217, field text_uthmani (Uthmani script; https://api.quran.com/api/v4/verses/by_key/2:217?fields=text_uthmani)
english: They ask you about the sacred month - about fighting therein. Say, "Fighting therein is great [sin], but averting [people] from the way of Allāh and disbelief in Him and [preventing access to] al-Masjid al-Ḥarām and the expulsion of its people therefrom are greater [evil] in the sight of Allāh. And fitnah is greater than killing." And they will continue to fight you until they turn you back from your religion if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion [to disbelief] and dies while he is a disbeliever - for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
translator: Saheeh International (quran.com translation id 20; footnote markers removed)
what_it_says: Fighting in the sacred month is a great sin, but driving people from the path of God, disbelief and expelling the people of the Sacred Mosque is worse, and fitna is worse than killing; the verse also says the Muslims will be fought until they are turned back from their religion if the enemy can.
